pages.spec: Know what you will study in KS3 ICT and how the department expects you to work
pages.summary: KS3 ICT teaches you what goes on behind the scenes of a computer and how to program one. Work and homework are shared on Google Classroom, and if you miss a lesson it is your job to catch up.

blocks.text: Welcome to the ICT department at Enniskillen Royal Grammar School! **[[ICT]]** stands for **Information and Communications Technology**. It is about how computers and other digital devices store, process and share information.

You will learn far more than how to switch on a games console or use an app on your phone. You will find out what actually goes on *behind the scenes* of a computer, and you will learn to write your own code. ERGS is a programming school, so by the end of KS3 you will have the skills to start building your own games, websites and apps.
*"You don't have to be great to start, but you have to start to be great."* Everyone starts at the beginning, so don't worry if some of your friends have used computers more than you.
What you will study in KS3

head: Year
What you will learn
rows: Introductions to ICT and activities: MySchool, Google Classroom, the computer contract, file management, safety, hardware and software, online safety and spreadsheets
Some new packages and applications, plus website design
Under the hood of a computer, plus an introduction to programming
blocks.caption: The KS3 ICT course at a glance

blocks.text: Google Classroom and MySchool

[[MySchool]] is the website you log in to with your school username and password. From it you can reach your school email and other tools. Your teacher (Mr Butler) uploads lessons, handouts and homework to **[[Google Classroom]]**. Every subject uses Google Classroom, and so do many school clubs and teams, so it is worth learning to use it well now. Take a note of your teacher's email address too, in case you cannot get into the resources.
If you are absent from class
If you miss an ICT lesson for any reason, it is **your responsibility** to catch up before the next lesson. That means:

items: Check whether any homework is due, and complete it.
Catch up on any work or notes you missed. If you don't understand them, see your teacher before the next lesson.
If there was a class test, see your teacher before the next lesson so you can sit it, or so a time can be arranged.

blocks.text: "I wasn't here last lesson" is **not** accepted as an excuse for missing homework. Ask a classmate, check Google Classroom or email your teacher.
If you know you will be absent (for example, for a school trip or a match), tell your teacher beforehand. You may be able to do the work early.

At the start of Year 8 you fill in a **Pupil Baseline Survey**. It is not a test. It simply tells your teacher what computer equipment you can use at home, so they can spot any problems early. Fill it in honestly using your c2k email address.

blocks.title: Key points
items: ICT = Information and Communications Technology.
Year 8: introductions; Year 9: new applications and web design; Year 10: under the hood and programming.
Lessons, handouts and homework are posted on Google Classroom.
If you are absent, you must catch up (homework, notes and any test) before the next lesson.

pages.spec: Know the school's Acceptable Use Policy and the top 10 rules of the computer room
pages.summary: Everyone must use the school network for learning and act responsibly. The Acceptable Use Policy and the top 10 computer room rules explain what is and is not allowed.

blocks.text: The school network is for your **education**. Every user is expected to act responsibly and to show consideration to others. Using the school's computers for anything that is not educational will bring about **[[sanctions|sanction]]** (punishments), and attempts to reach blocked sites are recorded on your account.
The Acceptable Use Policy

An **[[Acceptable Use Policy]]** (AUP) is a set of rules you agree to before you are allowed to use the computers. It keeps **you** safe and it keeps the **network and its data** safe. Before you can use a school computer you sign the **School Computer Contract**, which is your promise to follow these rules.

items: **Never** tell anyone your password.
Only log on to **your own** account, and **log off** when you leave a [[workstation]].
Do not download, store or install software on school computers.
Do not try to introduce a virus or any malicious (harmful) code to the network.
Do not access, download, create, store or send material that is indecent or obscene, or that brings the name of the school into disrepute (gives it a bad name).
Do not use public chat rooms or social networks in school.
Do not directly copy material from the internet and use it as your own work.

blocks.text: Top 10 rules of the computer room

Why
rows: Get permission to enter the labs
Ask a member of staff before you go in.
Use the bins, put bags under desks, tidy your desk and tuck chairs in.
Turn your screen off when asked
Do it immediately, the first time you are asked.
Do not move, unplug or take anything apart. Hacking is illegal.
It smells and can damage the equipment (this includes chewing gum).

Manage your files so they are easy to find.

blocks.caption: The top 10 rules of the computer room

blocks.text: There are a few more rules you will hear in lessons: do not change any settings on the computer, report any damage to the teacher, do not touch somebody else's computer, do not play games or surf the internet during a lesson, only use Google Classroom for educational purposes, and never send inappropriate or upsetting messages, because that is **cyberbullying**.
Logging in as a friend, even "for a laugh", breaks the rules. Anything done on that account looks like it was done by your friend.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The school network is for education only; misuse leads to sanctions.
Never share your password; only use your own account and always log off.
No downloading or installing software, no viruses, no offensive material, no chat rooms or social networks.
No food or drink in the computer room, keep it tidy, and only print when necessary.
You sign the School Computer Contract to agree to these rules.

pages.spec: Explain what a computer, a network and the internet are
pages.summary: A computer is a machine that stores and processes data by following instructions. A network is two or more computers joined so they can communicate and share. The internet is the biggest network of all, and nobody owns it.

blocks.text: What is a computer?

A **[[computer]]** is a type of machine. It is used for storing and processing **[[data]]** by following instructions given to it in a **program**. Because the program can be changed, the same computer can do lots of different jobs: a word processor one minute, a game the next.
A computer doesn't have a brain like a human, so it can't think or have ideas of its own. It only does exactly what its instructions tell it to, but it does that very fast and very accurately.
What is a network?

A **[[network]]** is made when **two or more computers are joined together**. This means they can communicate with each other and share things like **printers** and **files**. A single computer that doesn't share or send data with any other computer is not a network.

items: **The internet**: the biggest network in the world.
**Home WiFi**: your phone, laptop, console and smart TV all joined to your router.
**Gaming networks**: such as PlayStation Network or Xbox network, letting you play friends online.
**Social networks**: such as Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok or YouTube, which join people together online.

blocks.text: The internet

The **[[internet]]** is a **worldwide network**. It lets computers from all over the world communicate with each other, for example to send email, play online games and use social networks. A pupil in Enniskillen can play a game against someone in Australia because both consoles are connected to the internet.
Who owns the internet?
**Nobody** is in charge of the whole internet. This means almost anybody can put almost anything onto it, which can cause problems because offensive or untrue material can appear.
You are not invisible online. Every device connected to the internet has an address (an **IP address**), so the police can often trace who posted something, even from a fake account.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A computer stores and processes data by following a program; it cannot think for itself.
A network = two or more computers joined together to communicate and share.
Examples of networks: the internet, home WiFi, gaming networks, social networks.
The internet is a worldwide network; nobody owns or controls all of it.

pages.spec: Describe the school network, why you need a unique login and how to set a strong password
pages.summary: School workstations are controlled by a server on the C2k network. You log in with a unique User ID and a secret password, which should be strong: at least 8 characters mixing capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols.

blocks.text: The school network

All the computers on the school network are controlled by a main computer called a **[[server]]**. The server lets everyone save their files **centrally** (in one place, so you can reach them from any computer in school) and share things like **printers**. The computer you sit at and use is called a **[[workstation]]**.
In some networks there is a **switch** or **hub** in the centre that the workstations plug into. For now, we will always label the centre of a network diagram as the server.
Logging in
Every pupil can use the school network. It is called the **[[C2k]]** network, and it runs in schools throughout Northern Ireland. You have login details to tell the server who you are:

items: A **[[User ID]]**: this is **unique**, so no one else has the same one. It tells the server *who* you are.
A **[[password]]**: chosen by you, and only you should know it. It **proves** you are who you say you are.

blocks.text: Everyone needs a **unique login** so the network knows exactly who is using it. That way your files are kept private, nobody else can see or change your work, and anything done on an account can be traced back to the right person.
Setting a strong password

head: A strong password should…
A strong password should NOT…
rows: Be just a name (yours, your dog's or your team's)
Use some numbers and symbols like $, %, !
Be the same as your username
Be the same as any other password you have used

blocks.title: Worked example: making a password stronger
blocks.context: Jack supports Ballinamallard United and wants to use the password *ballinamallard*.
steps: It is just a name, and people who know Jack could guess it: **weak**.
Make it longer and mix the case: *Ballina-Mallard*.
Add numbers and symbols: *Ballina!Mallard_74*.
Better still, use three random words joined together: *Kettle7!Otter$Rain*.
blocks.answer: Kettle7!Otter$Rain is strong: over 8 characters, capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols, and not linked to Jack.

blocks.text: Never write the example passwords on this page down and use them. They are now public! Make up your own, and you may be asked to change it during the year.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The server controls the network, stores files centrally and shares printers; you use a workstation.
The school network is part of C2k, used across Northern Ireland.
Your User ID is unique; your password proves who you are and must stay secret.
Strong password: 8+ characters, capitals and lower case, numbers, symbols; not a name, not your username, not reused.

pages.spec: Explain the difference between files and folders, recognise common file extensions and organise work in a folder structure
pages.summary: Files hold your work; folders hold files. Using a sensible folder structure with meaningful names means you can always find your work quickly, keep backups easily and avoid saving the same file in several places.

blocks.text: Files and folders

A **[[file]]** is one piece of saved work, such as an essay, a photo or a song. A **[[folder]]** is a container that holds files (and other folders) so they are grouped and organised, just like the ring binders in your schoolbag hold your worksheets.

head: File
Folder
rows: One item of work or data
A container for files and other folders
A page (often coloured, showing the program)

blocks.text: File extensions

The **[[file extension]]** is the part after the dot at the end of a file name. It tells the computer what type of file it is and which program should open it. Microsoft Word documents end in **.docx**, Excel spreadsheets in **.xlsx** and PowerPoint presentations in **.pptx**.

head: File extension
What it stands for
Type of file
blocks.caption: Common file extensions and their meanings

head: Icon
Program
Typical extension
rows: Dark red square with an A
blocks.caption: Recognising Microsoft Office icons

blocks.text: Sorceress Alice's folder structure

Alice has a **[[root folder]]** called *Year 8*. Inside it are five subject folders: Science, Maths, ICT, English and History. Inside those are topic folders: **Science → Space**; **ICT → Spreadsheets, Databases**; **English → Poems, Haiku, Macbeth**. (Maths and History have no topic folders yet.)

blocks.title: Worked example: where should Alice save her files?
blocks.context: Use Alice's folder structure to decide where each file belongs.
steps: **Marks.xlsx** is an Excel spreadsheet, so it belongs in ICT's Spreadsheets folder: *Year 8 > ICT > Spreadsheets*.
Her two downloaded pictures (one .jpg and *Mars.gif*) are about planets, so they go in *Year 8 > Science > Space*.
Her new History topic needs a new folder: create *World War II* inside History, then save the Word document there: *Year 8 > History > World War II > The Trenches.docx*.
blocks.answer: Spreadsheets folder; Space folder; a new World War II folder inside History holding The Trenches.docx.

blocks.text: Why organise your files?

items: It is much **easier to find** files: you always know where to look and never waste time wondering where to save something.
You can easily **direct someone**, such as your teacher, to a file.
It is easier to keep **[[backups|backup]]**.
You don't save files in several places, or save the same file again because you can't find the first copy.
It is **more efficient**: less storage is wasted on duplicate copies, and you find files quickly when time is short.

blocks.text: In school, save work in your own area on the network, inside a sensible path such as *Year 8 > ICT > Unit 1*. If the folders aren't there, create them, and always give files **meaningful names** like *Email Quiz.docx*, not *Document1.docx*.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A file is one item of work; a folder is a container for files and folders.
File extensions (.docx, .jpg, .mp3…) show the type of file.
Organise files in a structure: root folder > subject > topic.
Organised files are quicker to find, easier to back up and don't waste storage.

pages.spec: Explain what email is, what you need to use it, and the rules of netiquette
pages.summary: Email is electronic mail sent between computers over the internet. You need an account, email software and internet access. Good netiquette means being polite, always using a subject line, avoiding capitals and text language.

blocks.text: **[[Email]]** stands for **electronic mail**. It is a message sent from one computer to another over the internet.
What you need to use email

head: You need…
Examples
rows: Gmail, Yahoo, AOL, Hotmail/Outlook.com, or your school C2k account
Outlook, webmail in a browser, Thunderbird
From an internet provider such as BT, Virgin Media, TalkTalk or Plusnet
blocks.caption: The three things you need to send email

blocks.text: Netiquette

Just like sending a letter, sending an email follows rules. Email is a fairly **formal** way to message someone, so it should be professional. **[[Netiquette]]** (net + etiquette) is how you should behave when sending emails and using the internet:

items: **Be polite.**
**Never forget the subject line**: whoever receives your email needs to know what it is about.
**Do not type in ALL CAPITALS**: it looks like you are SHOUTING.
**Don't use text language** (like *c u l8r*), not even when emailing friends.
Show you are joking with a smiley :) . [[Emoticons|Emoticon]] are fine in informal emails to friends, but not in formal emails to a teacher or a boss.

blocks.text: Sender and recipient

The **[[sender]]** is the person who sends the email. The **[[recipient]]** is the person who receives it. When a message is sent, a copy is kept in the sender's **Sent** folder and the message appears in the recipient's **[[inbox]]**. The recipient opens it to read it.
Your school email address

Your school email address is the **username you use to log in to the school computers**, followed by **@c2ken.net**. For example, if your username is *aperson123*, your email address is **aperson123@c2ken.net**.
Write your school email address in your planner so you always have it.
Reading your school email

The school uses **Microsoft Outlook**. In your inbox, new (unread) emails have a **blue bar**, the **sender** is shown in **bold**, the **subject** is in blue and a **preview** of the start of the message appears underneath. You can also see when it was sent. Double-click an email to open and read it in full.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Email = electronic mail, sent between computers over the internet.
You need an email account, email software and internet access.
Netiquette: be polite, always add a subject, no ALL CAPS, no text language.
Sender sends; recipient receives the email in their inbox.
School email = your login username + @c2ken.net.

pages.spec: Send an email from school, and use CC, BCC, reply, forward and attachments correctly
pages.summary: You send school email through MySchool > Office 365 > Outlook. CC sends a visible copy, BCC a hidden copy. Replying (RE:) goes back to the sender, forwarding (FW:) passes the email on, and a paperclip shows an attachment.

blocks.text: Sending an email in school

items: Open the internet and log in to **MySchool**.
Click on **Office 365**.
Select **Outlook**.
Select **New Message**.
Type the email address of the recipient, e.g. a friend in your class.
Add a **meaningful subject line**.
Type your message using suitable language, e.g. tell them a little about yourself: your favourite team, a film or music artist you like, a game you recently played.
**Sign off** with your name so they know who it is from.
Click **Send**.

blocks.text: CC and BCC
Under the **To** box you will see **CC**, and sometimes **BCC**. These are useful when emailing more than one person.

head: CC (carbon copy)
BCC (blind carbon copy)
rows: Copying your form teacher into an email to Mr Butler
A club newsletter sent to 1000 people, so nobody's address is shown to the others

blocks.text: BCC is a bit like a company sending a newsletter: you get your copy, but you can't see the 999 other people who were sent it, and they can't see your address.
Replying and forwarding

**[[Replying|Reply]]** sends a message **back** to the person who sent the email to you. The address is filled in automatically and **RE:** appears in front of the subject. **[[Forwarding|Forward]]** sends the email **on** to someone else. **FW:** (or **Fwd:**) appears in front of the subject.

blocks.title: Worked example: Alex, Jack and Robert
blocks.context: Alex sends an email with the subject *Rugby training* to Jack.
steps: Jack receives it in his inbox. Alex is the sender; Jack is the recipient.
Jack **replies** to Alex: the email goes back to Alex with the subject *RE: Rugby training*.
Jack **forwards** it to Robert: Robert gets Alex's message with the subject *FW: Rugby training*.
blocks.answer: Reply = back to the sender (RE:). Forward = on to someone new (FW:).

blocks.text: Attachments

An **[[attachment]]** is a file sent with an email, such as a Word document or a photo. When an email has an attachment, a **paperclip icon** appears next to it. You can open the email and then open or save the attachment. To add one, click **Attach** (the paperclip) in a new message and choose the file.

blocks.title: Worked example: the Sending Email practical quiz
blocks.context: You save a Word document called *Quick Quiz* in *Year 8 > ICT > Email*, answer six questions in it and email it to your teacher as an attachment.
steps: Q1 What does email stand for? **Electronic mail.**
Q2 Difference between replying and forwarding? **Replying sends the email back to the person who sent it; forwarding sends it on to someone else.**

Q3 Difference between the internet and the WWW? **The internet is the physical network of connected computers (hardware); the WWW is the collection of websites on it (the software you reach with a browser).**
Q4 What does netiquette mean? **How you should behave when sending emails and using the internet.**
Q5 Three tasks search engines perform? **Crawling, indexing and retrieval.**
Q6 How to add an attachment? **Click the paperclip/Attach button and choose the file.**
For full marks the email itself also needs a professional subject line, a suitable attachment name, a greeting, a clear message and your name to sign off.
blocks.answer: A good email: subject + greeting + message + sign-off + correctly named attachment.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Send school email: MySchool > Office 365 > Outlook > New Message.
CC = visible copy; BCC = hidden copy.
Reply goes back to the sender (RE:); forward goes to someone new (FW:).
A paperclip icon means the email has an attachment.

check.q: Jack receives an email from Alex and sends it on to Robert. What has Jack done?
check.why: Sending it on to someone new is forwarding.

check.q: What appears in front of the subject when you reply?
check.why: RE: shows it is a reply.

check.q: A club secretary emails 200 members and doesn't want them to see each other's addresses. Which box should she use?
check.why: BCC hides recipients from each other.

check.q: What does a paperclip icon next to an email mean?
check.why: The paperclip shows an attachment.

practice.q: Explain the difference between replying to and forwarding an email.
practice.a: Replying sends a message back to the person who sent you the email (1); forwarding sends the email on to someone else / a new person (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between CC and BCC.
practice.a: Both send a copy of the email to another person (1), but with BCC the other recipients cannot see who was copied in, whereas with CC they can (1).

pages.spec: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web, and how search engines work
pages.summary: The internet is the physical network of connected computers (hardware); the World Wide Web is the websites stored on it (software), viewed in a browser. Search engines use algorithms to crawl, index and retrieve web pages.

blocks.text: The internet and the WWW are not the same thing

head: The internet
The World Wide Web (WWW)
rows: A massive global network of computers linked together
The collection of millions of websites stored on the internet
Email, online gaming, video calls, the web and more
Through a connection such as WiFi or broadband

blocks.text: The **[[internet]]** is the **hardware**: millions of computers linked by cables (including under the sea!), routers and satellites. The **[[World Wide Web]]** is just **one service** that runs on the internet. You view it with a **[[web browser]]** such as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox or Safari.
Think of the internet as the **roads** and the WWW as the **shops** you visit using those roads. Email and online gaming also use the roads, but they are not shops on the web.
Search engines
A **[[search engine]]**, such as Google or Bing, helps you find pages on the WWW. Search engines use complex **[[algorithm|algorithms]]** (sets of step-by-step rules) to do three tasks:

head: Task
What happens
rows: Programs called web crawlers (or spiders) follow links to discover websites.
Each website is analysed and stored in a huge database called an index.
When you search, you receive a list of relevant web pages, with the most relevant at the top.
blocks.caption: The three tasks of a search engine

blocks.text: The web is enormous. In 2020 the indexed web held at least **6.51 billion** pages, and back in 2013 Google said its index already held information about 30 trillion pages and used 100 million gigabytes of storage. It has grown hugely since.
The top result is not always true! Anyone can publish on the web, so check information on more than one trustworthy site.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Internet = global network of connected computers (hardware).
WWW = the websites on the internet (software), viewed in a web browser.
Search engines crawl, index and retrieve web pages using algorithms.
The most relevant results appear at the top, but always check they are reliable.

nodes.label: Crawling
nodes.detail: Web crawlers follow links to discover websites.

nodes.label: Indexing
nodes.detail: Each page is analysed and stored in a huge database (the index).

nodes.label: You search
nodes.detail: You type keywords such as 'Enniskillen Castle opening times'.

nodes.label: Retrieval
nodes.detail: You get a list of relevant pages, the most relevant at the top.

check.q: Which statement is correct?
o: The internet and the WWW are the same thing
The internet is a type of web browser
The WWW is a collection of websites stored on the internet
Email is part of the WWW
check.why: The WWW is the websites; the internet is the network.

check.q: Which of these is a web browser?
check.why: Chrome is a browser; Bing is a search engine.

check.q: In which search engine task is a website analysed and stored in a database?
check.why: Indexing stores pages in a huge database.

check.q: What is a web crawler used for?
check.why: Crawlers discover websites.

practice.q: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
practice.a: The internet is a global network of connected computers / the physical hardware (1); the WWW is the collection of websites stored on the internet, viewed in a browser / the software (1).

practice.q: Name and describe the **three** tasks a search engine performs.
practice.a: Crawling: websites are discovered (1); indexing: websites are analysed and stored in a huge database (1); retrieval: you receive a list of relevant web pages for your search (1).

pages.spec: Describe what a computer virus can do and how to avoid one
pages.summary: A virus is a harmful program designed to damage a computer or make it unreliable: corrupting and deleting files, stealing personal information or slowing it down. Avoid them by not opening unknown attachments, using up-to-date anti-virus software and only downloading safely.

blocks.text: A computer **[[virus]]** is a program designed to **deliberately damage** a computer system or make it **unreliable**. Like a cold virus, it spreads from one computer to another, often hidden inside an email attachment, a download or a USB stick.
What can a virus do?

items: **Corrupt** (scramble) files and folders so they won't open.
**Delete** data.
**Steal** your personal information, such as passwords.
Infect your computer so it **slows down** or **stops working**.

blocks.text: How to avoid viruses

head: Do this…
Because…
rows: Don't open email attachments from people you don't know
Attachments are one of the most common ways viruses spread.
Install anti-virus software and keep it up to date
New viruses appear every day; old anti-virus software won't recognise them.
Only download files from known, safe sites, with permission from a parent or guardian
Free games, mods and films from unknown sites often hide viruses.
Scan USB memory sticks before opening files on them
A stick that has been in an infected computer can carry the virus to yours.
blocks.caption: Ways to stay virus-free

blocks.text: **[[Anti-virus software]]** scans files, emails and USB sticks, looking for known viruses, and removes or quarantines (locks away) anything it finds. This is one reason why you must never try to install software or plug in unknown devices on the school network.

blocks.title: Worked example: should Ciara open it?
blocks.context: Ciara gets an email from an address she doesn't recognise. The subject is *You've won a free PS5!!!* and it has an attachment called *claim_prize.exe*.
steps: She doesn't know the sender, so this is a warning sign.
The offer is too good to be true, which is another warning sign.
The attachment is a program (.exe), which could install a virus if opened.
blocks.answer: No. Ciara should not open the attachment, should not reply, and should tell an adult or delete the email.

blocks.text: Never try to bring a virus onto the school network, even "as a joke". It breaks the Acceptable Use Policy and can be against the law.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A virus is a program designed to damage a computer or make it unreliable.
Viruses can corrupt or delete files, steal personal information and slow a computer down.
Don't open attachments from strangers.
Use up-to-date anti-virus software, download only from safe sites with permission, and scan USB sticks.

check.q: Which of these is something a virus can do?
check.why: Viruses can steal personal data.

check.q: Why must anti-virus software be kept up to date?
o: So it can recognise new viruses
check.why: New viruses are created all the time.

check.q: A friend gives you a USB stick with photos from the school trip. What should you do first?
check.why: Scan USB sticks before using them.

check.q: Which email attachment is the most suspicious?
o: free_game.exe from someone you don't know
check.why: An unknown program from a stranger is high risk.

practice.q: State **two** ways a virus can damage a computer.
practice.a: Any two: corrupting files/folders (1); deleting data (1); stealing personal information (1); slowing the computer down or stopping it working (1).

practice.q: Describe **three** ways to protect a computer from viruses.
practice.a: Don't open email attachments from people you don't know (1); install anti-virus software and keep it up to date (1); only download from known safe sites with permission (1); scan USB memory sticks (1). Any three.

glossary.def: Short for Information and Communications Technology: using computers and other digital devices to store, process and share information.
An online space where your teachers post lessons, handouts and homework, and where you hand in work.
The online portal you log in to with your school username and password to reach your school email (Office 365), Google Classroom and other tools.
A set of rules that everyone must agree to before using the school's computers, to keep users, the network and data safe.
A punishment or consequence for breaking a rule, such as losing access to the network.
A computer on a network that a person sits at and uses, such as the PC in front of you in the ICT room.
A machine that stores and processes data by following a set of instructions called a program.
Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, text or pictures, before they are given meaning.
Two or more computers joined together so they can communicate and share things such as files and printers.
A massive worldwide network of computers linked together by physical hardware such as cables and routers.
A main computer that controls a network and provides services, such as storing everyone's files and sharing printers.
The network used by schools all across Northern Ireland; your school login and @c2ken.net email come from it.
Your unique username that tells the network who you are; nobody else has the same one.
A secret word or set of characters, known only to you, that proves you are who you say you are.
A password that is hard to guess or crack: at least 8 characters with capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols.
A single item of saved work or data, such as a document, photo or song, with a name and a file extension.
A container used to group and organise files (and other folders) so they are easy to find.
The letters after the dot at the end of a file name, such as .docx or .jpg, which show what type of file it is.
The top folder in a folder structure, which all the other folders are stored inside.
A spare copy of your files kept in a different place, so you can get them back if the originals are lost or damaged.
Short for electronic mail: a message sent from one computer to another over the internet.
The rules of good behaviour when sending emails and using the internet (from 'net' + 'etiquette').
The person who sends an email.
The person who receives an email.
The folder in your email where new messages you receive arrive.
A small face made from characters or a picture, such as :) , used to show feelings in a message.
Carbon copy: anyone in the CC box gets a copy of the email, and everyone can see they were copied in.
Blind carbon copy: anyone in the BCC box gets a copy of the email, but the other recipients cannot see they were sent it.
Sending an email back to the person who sent it to you; RE: appears before the subject.
Sending an email you received on to someone else; FW: appears before the subject.
A file, such as a document or photo, sent along with an email; shown by a paperclip icon.
The collection of millions of websites and web pages stored on computers connected to the internet; often called the WWW or the web.
Software used to view websites on the World Wide Web, such as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox or Safari.
A website, such as Google or Bing, that finds web pages matching the words you type in.
A harmful program that copies itself and is designed to damage files, steal information or make a computer unreliable.
A program that scans files, emails and USB sticks to find and remove viruses; it must be kept up to date.
